course_description:
Introduction to nanomaterials with an emphasis on their fabrication, structures, properties and application

With the rapid development of nanoscience and nanotechnology, nanomaterials have attracted great attention based on their fundamental scientific importance and potential technological applications. This course is an introduction to nanomaterials, providing students an updated overview on the unique properties (mechanical, physical and chemical) of nanomaterials and their key design and manufacturing techniques and potential applications. This course will also briefly introduce several key tools and techniques for characterising nanomaterials. Students will learn these technniques in relation to the manufacturing and characterisation of nanomaterials through lectures, lab practices, oral presentations and independent assessments. After successful completion of the course, students will have a good understanding of the fundamentals of various functional nanomaterials, their properties, advanced characterisation processes and their applications with case studies.

course_aims: The course aims to provide a fundamental understanding of a wide range of functional nanomaterials with focus on their design, manufacturing andﾠcharacterisationﾠtechniques to become familiar with crystal structures and how they affect the unique properties of nanomaterials, as well as their advanced applications in engineering, energy, environments, and health. The course alsoﾠprovides a platform for students to gain practical skills in analysis and evaluation through oral presentations, as well as design and implementation of scientific writing.ﾠ

learning_outcomes.description: Explain the differences between nanomaterials and their bulk counterparts in terms of properties and applications, and apply this understanding to the design of fabrication and characterisation strategies for high-performance nanomaterials.

Apply X-ray crystallography techniques to determine the microstructures of nanomaterials and evaluate experimental data against peer-reviewed literature to identify the phase of unknown materials and justify conclusions.

Apply scanning and transmission electron microscopy techniques to determine the microstructures of nanomaterials and interpret the resulting observations in relation to material behaviour and application.

Design, fabricate, and characterise functional nanomaterials, including porous gold nanostructures and magnetic nanocomposites, and analyse their optical and magnetic properties for practical applications.
Select appropriate magnetic and optical nanostructures to meet the requirements of designed applications.
Design strategies to enhance the mechanical properties and performance of selected nanocellulose for targeted applications.
Explain the physical concepts and phenomena underpinning nanocatalysts and describe their current and potential applications.

Describe the applications of porous carbon, semiconducting, and porous nanostructured materials in medicine, energy, agriculture, and the environment, and fabricate, characterise, and improve their performance for targeted applications.

Construct literature reviews through critical evaluation of existing research on nanomaterial systems, and communicate experimental outcomes and research findings using the norms and conventions of the discipline.

Collaboratively engage in nanomaterials fabrication and characterisation, demonstrating effective teamwork, technical problem-solving, and the ability to independently collect, analyse, and critically evaluate experimental and literature data to address challenges in nanomaterials manufacturing and applications.

assessment_details.title: Development and characterisation of nanoporous gold film
assessment_details.other_conditions: Student specific. See the conditions definitions
assessment_details.task_description: The project will be conducted over four sessions. The first session will involve the deposition of a mesoporous gold (Au) thin film. The subsequent three sessions will focus on characterisation of the film using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM). These activities will be delivered as in-person laboratory demonstrations. Students will be provided with the experimental data generated during the demonstrations and will be required to independently analyse the results and prepare an individual report. The report is due to be submitted 4:00pm on 14 September. Although this project will be conducted in groups, each student is required to write an independent report.
